html:
Armenia is the land of the Armenian people in the highlands between the Black Sea, the Caspian and the upper Tigris and Euphrates, around Mount Ararat. Today's Republic of Armenia covers only a small part of the historic land. On the map it appears off and on from 323 BCE to now.

It grew from the land of Urartu. After Alexander, local dynasties ruled, and under Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BCE Armenia briefly held an empire from the Caspian to Syria before it bowed to Rome.

Two events set its identity:

  • Around 301, King Tiridates III made Armenia the first state to adopt Christianity.
  • Around 405, the monk Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet, which is still used.

For most of its history Armenia was a borderland between empires: Rome and Persia, which divided it in 387, then Byzantium and the Arab caliphs, then Turks, Mongols, Ottomans and Persians. It had moments of independence, such as the Bagratid kingdom with its capital at Ani in the 900s and 1000s, and a kingdom in Cilicia on the Mediterranean from 1198 to 1375.

In the 1800s Russia took the east. In the Ottoman west, the Armenian genocide of 1915 to 1923 killed about a million Armenians or more and destroyed their life in Anatolia. A short independent republic in 1918 fell to the Bolsheviks in 1920, and Armenia became a Soviet republic. It became independent again in 1991 as the Soviet Union broke up, and has since fought Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian populated region that Azerbaijan retook in 2020 and 2023.
